name: Cornflower
summary: A cool-season annual with vivid flowers useful in pollinator and cutting gardens. NC State Extension supports early indoor starts or fall direct sowing in mild-winter regions; it can reseed readily, so deadheading depends on whether seed spread is wanted.

identity.guidance: Kew POWO accepts Centaurea cyanus L. NC State lists cornflower, bluebottle and bachelor's button as common names. No cultivar or color strain is assigned.

growth.short: Cool-season annual with blue, pink or white flower forms
growth.guidance: NC State describes a cool-season annual with an erect, branching form, edible flowers, and value for butterflies and other wildlife. Its general species profile does not identify the color or height of an unnamed seed packet.

cultivation.short: Grow in sun; shade can increase flopping
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun to light shade and medium moisture in well-drained soil, and notes stems can flop in excessive shade. This regional outdoor guidance does not establish indoor grow-light needs or hydroponic suitability.

care.guidance: NC State notes that cornflower can reseed and naturalize. Remove spent heads when limiting seed spread is the goal; leave some if supporting wildlife or collecting seed is intended. Taller plants may need support where they cannot lean on neighboring plants.

harvestUse.short: Cut: about one-third of the spray open
harvestUse.guidance: For cut-flower sprays, Rutgers lists harvest when roughly one-third of the flowers have opened. This is species-named production guidance, not a maturity date or cultivar-specific vase-life promise. NC State identifies the flowers as edible; that does not establish food safety for plants exposed to pesticides or other unsuitable treatments.

problems.short: No major pests noted; watch for wilt, rot, rust and aphids
problems.guidance: NC State reports no serious insect or disease problems but lists wilt, rots, rust, aphids and mealybugs as possible issues. These are monitoring cues, not a claim that every cornflower will experience them.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor soil guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: NC State describes an erect form; stems may flop in shade.

height.reason: The extension range spans species forms and is not assigned to an unspecified packet.

spread.reason: No single cultivar or container footprint is specified.

spacing.reason: Landscape spacing is not equivalent to Garden pod capacity.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Strawflower
summary: An Australian-origin flower grown for long-lasting fresh and dried blooms. Kew accepts Xerochrysum bracteatum; NC State notes that many named cultivars do not come true from seed, so this species-level identity does not imply a cultivar.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Xerochrysum bracteatum and lists Bracteantha bracteata and Helichrysum bracteatum as synonyms. No cultivar is assigned; NC State specifically warns that many cultivars do not grow true from seed.

growth.short: Flowering annual or short-lived tender perennial
growth.guidance: NC State describes strawflower as an annual or short-lived tender perennial with papery bracts that retain shape and color when dried. Heights vary substantially across cultivars, so no single mature dimension is assigned to this unnamed species-level entry.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained soil; tolerate some light shade
cultivation.guidance: NC State reports average to dry, well-drained soil and full sun to partial shade for its regional landscape guidance. Illinois Extension recommends full sun for its Illinois garden context. Neither source establishes hydroponic suitability.

care.short: Deadhead for branching and more blooms; taller forms may need support
care.guidance: NC State says regular deadheading may encourage side shoots and more blooms, while taller forms may need staking. These are general species/cultivar-group recommendations; the response of an unnamed strain is not guaranteed.

harvestUse.guidance: For cut stems, Utah State recommends harvest when three to four layers of bracts are open and the center is just becoming visible; leaving at least three nodes supports regrowth for later cuts in its Intermountain West production context. Much earlier cutting risks bent-neck wilting; later cutting reduces vase life. These are crop-production cues, not cultivar dimensions. NC State and Illinois Extension describe fresh and dried cut-flower use; color and stem length vary by cultivar.

problems.short: Downy mildew is a reported risk
problems.guidance: NC State lists downy mildew as a possible problem and reports no known insect problems in its profile. Absence of listed insect problems is not a guarantee of pest-free growth.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Landscape and cut-flower soil guidance does not demonstrate hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: NC State describes erect stems and a clumping habit; cultivar dimensions vary.

height.reason: Published height varies by cultivar and is not assigned to an unnamed identity.

spacing.reason: Outdoor cut-flower spacing is not Garden pod capacity.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor grow-light tier.
